title: AI + Security & Safety — Don Bosco Durai

primary.label: AI Platforms & Developer Tooling

summary:
Bosco Durai introduces his background as co-founder and CTO of Privacera, creator of Apache Ranger (the open-source data governance standard for Big Data used by AWS, GCP, Azure), and leader of PAIG.ai, an open-source project for security, safety, and governance of GenAI applications and AI agents. He standardizes terminology: AI agents are autonomous systems that reason independently, create workflows, and call tasks; tasks are specific actions that may use LLMs, RAGs, or tools; tools are functions for accessing the internet, databases, or service APIs; memory is context shared within agents, tasks, and tools.

A key architectural vulnerability is that most agent frameworks run as a single process, meaning tools, tasks, and agents share credentials (often super-admin service users) and prompts, allowing cross-access. This creates zero-trust issues. Additionally, agents' autonomy introduces "unknown unknowns"—non-deterministic behavior with high attack vectors compared to traditional software. Challenges include unauthorized access, data leakage, safety/trust issues from unreliable models or prompt tampering, and compliance/governance gaps. Bosco shares an anecdote about a top-three credit bureau treating AI agents like human users, requiring onboarding, training, and adherence to regulations before production deployment.

He proposes three layers of defense: (1) Evals—security and safety-focused evaluations producing a risk score for production readiness, covering test coverage, vulnerability scanning, prompt injection testing, data leakage, unauthorized actions, and runaway agent scenarios; (2) Enforcement—authentication, authorization, identity propagation across the entire agent→task→tool chain so correct policies are enforced at the point of data access or API calls, and approvals with thresholds and human-in-the-loop guardrails; (3) Observability—monitoring real-world usage because models change rapidly, agent frameworks evolve, third-party libraries behave differently, and user inputs are subjective. Since per-request monitoring isn't feasible at scale, organizations need thresholds, metrics, failure rate tracking, and anomaly detection akin to user behavior analytics in traditional security—though Bosco notes this is still in early stages for agents. He recaps the approach as preemptive (vulnerability evals and risk scores), proactive enforcement (guardrails, sandbox), and observability for near-real-time security posture. He announces PAIG.ai is open-sourced, seeking design partners and contributors (contact: bosco@paig.ai or LinkedIn).
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction & Terminology
sections.summary: Bosco introduces himself as co-founder and CTO of Privacera, creator of Apache Ranger, and leader of PAIG.ai open-source project. He standardizes terminology: agents are autonomous reasoning systems, tasks are specific actions, tools are functions for external access, and memory is shared context. He notes agents, tasks, and tools can access LLMs, RAGs, databases, and service APIs.

sections.title: Security Challenges in Agent Frameworks
sections.summary: Bosco explains that most agent frameworks run as a single process, sharing credentials (often super-admin service users) and prompts across components, creating zero-trust vulnerabilities. Agent autonomy introduces 'unknown unknowns' and non-deterministic behavior. Challenges include unauthorized access, data leakage, safety/trust issues, and compliance gaps. He shares a credit bureau anecdote where AI agents are treated like human users requiring onboarding, training, and regulatory adherence.

sections.title: Three-Layer Defense Approach
sections.summary: Bosco proposes three layers of defense: (1) Evals to determine production readiness via risk scores, including security and safety-focused evaluations; (2) Enforcement with strong implementation of authentication, authorization, and controls; (3) Observability to monitor real-world usage since many variables can't be caught during development.

sections.title: Evals for Security and Safety
sections.summary: Bosco details eval requirements mirroring traditional software development: test coverage, vulnerability scanning for Docker containers and third-party software, pen testing, prompt injection testing, data leakage testing (e.g., HR agent accessing other employees' salary), unauthorized action testing, and runaway agent testing. The goal is to produce a risk score determining production readiness.

sections.title: Enforcement: Authentication, Authorization, and Approvals
sections.summary: Bosco covers enforcement in a zero-trust environment: authentication prevents impersonation; authorization ensures role-based access control where agents don't exceed their roles and user permissions are enforced when accessing databases or APIs on behalf of users. Approvals can be agent-based with thresholds and human-in-the-loop guardrails when exceeding limits. He emphasizes authentication and authorization are critical and interrelated.

sections.title: Observability, Recap, and PAIG.ai Open Source
sections.summary: Bosco explains that user identity must be propagated across the entire agent→task→tool chain to enforce correct access policies at the point of data access or API calls. He details observability challenges unique to agents: models change rapidly, agent frameworks evolve, third-party libraries behave differently, and user inputs are subjective and non-deterministic. Since per-request monitoring isn't feasible at scale, organizations need thresholds, metrics, failure rate tracking, and anomaly detection similar to user behavior analytics in traditional security—though he notes this is still in early stages for agents. He recaps the approach as preemptive (evals and risk scores), proactive enforcement (guardrails, sandbox), and observability for near-real-time security posture. He announces PAIG.ai is open-sourced, seeking design partners and contributors (contact: bosco@paig.ai or LinkedIn).

limitations: Most agent frameworks today run as a single process, making credentials and prompts accessible across components
Agents are non-deterministic by definition, introducing 'unknown unknowns' that are hard to anticipate
Observability is critical because many variables cannot be caught during development or initial testing
Cannot monitor every request at scale—thresholds and metrics are needed instead
Anomaly detection for agents is still in early stages compared to traditional security user behavior analytics
AI Engineers are still in early stages and often overlook compliance and governance needed for enterprise readiness
